title: Schengen Visa Travel Insurance: The €30,000 Minimum, Zero-Deductible Rule, and Common Rejections
excerpt: Under Article 15 of the EU Visa Code, every applicant for a short-stay Schengen visa must hold compliant travel medical insurance. Here are the mandatory coverage heads, the zero-deductible requirement that catches most applicants, and the reasons consulates reject policies.
author: WBI Editorial Team
keyTakeaways: Regulation (EC) No 810/2009 (EU Visa Code, Article 15) mandates minimum medical cover of €30,000 (or $50,000 equivalent).
The policy must explicitly cover all 29 Schengen Area countries, not just the primary country of application.
Repatriation of remains and emergency medical evacuation are mandatory statutory lines; a policy covering medical treatment alone will be rejected.
A deductible or excess can trigger immediate rejection at German, French, and Swiss consulates, which require zero-deductible coverage.
The policy must cover the entire intended period of stay, plus a recommended 15-day grace period.
Purchasing from an insurer with a direct representative office in Europe ensures smooth claim clearance and consular recognition.

sections.heading: The statutory requirement
sections.body: Article 15 of the European Parliament Visa Code (Regulation EC No 810/2009) makes travel medical insurance a non-negotiable statutory condition for issuing a uniform short-stay Schengen Visa (Type C). A visa cannot be stamped without verifying the insurance certificate.
paragraphs: While many travelers view travel insurance as an optional accessory, European consulates treat it as a mandatory public-health indemnity to ensure foreign visitors do not burden state healthcare systems during emergencies.

Consular officers scrutinize the insurance declaration page with specific checklist criteria. Failing any single one of the statutory requirements results in visa denial or an administrative hold requiring you to buy a new compliant policy on the spot.

sections.heading: The mandatory checklist: what the policy must contain
sections.body: Your insurance certificate must explicitly state each of the following conditions on the primary schedule submitted to VFS, TLScontact, or the consulate.

rows: Must cover emergency hospitalisation and outpatient care
Must state 'All Schengen States' or list all 29 members
Emergency medical transfer to the nearest appropriate facility
Return of mortal remains to country of residence in case of death
Consulates frequently reject policies with $50–$100 co-pays
Must match flight reservations; 15-day buffer recommended
table.caption: The statutory coverage checklist mandated under Article 15 of the EU Visa Code.

callout.label: The 29 Schengen Countries
callout.text: The Schengen Area includes 29 member states following the accession of Bulgaria and Romania: Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Italy, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland.

sections.heading: The zero-deductible pitfall: why cheap policies get rejected
sections.body: The single most common reason a travel insurance certificate is rejected during visa processing is the presence of an 'excess' or 'deductible'.
paragraphs: Budget travel policies often reduce upfront premiums by inserting a $50, $100, or €100 deductible, meaning the traveler pays the first portion of any claim out of pocket.

Consulates of several major Schengen states — particularly Germany, France, Switzerland, and the Czech Republic — interpret the Visa Code strictly: the full €30,000 minimum cover must be guaranteed by the insurer without any initial financial hurdle imposed on the claimant. If the certificate lists a non-zero deductible, consular officers regularly mark the insurance invalid.
When purchasing travel insurance for a European visa, verify that the 'Deductible / Excess' field on the certificate explicitly reads 'Nil', '$0', or '€0'.

sections.heading: The 15-day validity buffer rule
sections.body: Under Article 15(2) of the Visa Code, multiple-entry and single-entry visas carry specific duration requirements.
bullets: Single-entry visa applicants: The insurance must cover the exact dates between arrival and departure from the Schengen zone.

The recommended 15-day buffer: Most European embassies (such as the German Missions and French Consulates) strongly recommend or require the insurance policy validity to exceed the travel duration by 15 days, allowing flexibility if return flights are rescheduled.

Multiple-entry visa applicants: Applicants must hold valid insurance covering the period of their first intended visit and sign the statement on the visa application form declaring they will purchase compliant insurance for subsequent visits.

sections.heading: Common reasons consulates reject travel policies
sections.body: Consular visa officers review thousands of certificates weekly and identify non-compliant schedules immediately.
bullets: Listing a single country instead of the Schengen Area: If you apply at the French Embassy and your policy states 'Valid in France only', it will be rejected. It must explicitly cover all Schengen States.
Exclusion of COVID-19 or viral emergencies: While COVID travel restrictions have eased, the medical policy must not exclude treatment for epidemic diseases.
Reimbursement-only clause without emergency assistance: The policy must provide an 24/7 international emergency assistance helpline with direct cashless settlement capability for European hospitals.
Currency mismatch: If the certificate expresses coverage in local currency (e.g. INR or AED), the amount must clearly convert to at least €30,000 at current exchange rates.

Unaccredited insurer: Some embassies maintain a public list of accredited insurance providers in specific source markets (such as India, UAE, and Pakistan). Policies purchased from unrecognised offshore brokers are denied.

sections.heading: What to do if your visa application is delayed or rejected
sections.body: If your visa is rejected or processing is delayed past your planned departure date, compliant travel insurance policies allow cancellation or date modification.
paragraphs: Almost all major insurers provide a full premium refund (minus a nominal administrative fee of €5 to €15) if you provide the official embassy visa rejection letter before the policy start date.

If your visa is approved but issuance is delayed, request a date endorsement from your insurer to shift the coverage window to match your rescheduled flight dates before crossing European border control.

faq.question: What is the minimum insurance amount for a Schengen visa?
faq.answer: €30,000 (thirty thousand euros), or the exact equivalent in US dollars (typically $50,000) or local currency, as mandated by Regulation (EC) No 810/2009.

faq.question: Does Schengen visa insurance require zero deductible?
faq.answer: Yes. Most Schengen consulates (notably Germany, France, and Switzerland) require a zero deductible (€0 excess). Policies with a deductible (e.g. $50 or $100) are frequently rejected by visa processing centers.

faq.question: Does my credit card travel insurance qualify for a Schengen visa?
faq.answer: It can qualify, but only if your card provider issues an official insurance certificate explicitly naming you, stating €30,000+ medical cover, valid across all Schengen countries, including medical evacuation and repatriation of remains. Generic card benefit brochures are not accepted.

faq.question: Are Bulgaria and Romania covered under Schengen travel insurance?
faq.answer: Yes. Both Bulgaria and Romania joined the Schengen Area. Any travel insurance policy specifying 'All Schengen States' automatically covers both nations.

faq.question: Can I cancel my travel insurance if my Schengen visa is rejected?
faq.answer: Yes. Most reputable insurance providers will issue a full premium refund if you submit the official embassy visa rejection letter prior to the policy start date.
